Double-shifted value indices (#124)

Redoes [#121](https://github.com/binius-zk/binius.xyz/pull/121) from
`main` in light of the reworked shift reduction (#122, #123). The
double-shifted value index notion carries over; the protocol around it
is new.

## Constraint system

A shifted value index names a prover word together with an **inner**
shift $(\text{op}_1, s_1)$ and an **outer** shift $(\text{op}_2, s_2)$
applied in sequence:

$$\textsf{val}(y, \text{op}_1, s_1, \text{op}_2, s_2) =
\text{op}_2\bigl(\text{op}_1(w[y], s_1), s_2\bigr)$$

Since $s = 0$ is the identity for every operation, single shifts and raw
words are the special cases $s_2 = 0$ and $s_1 = s_2 = 0$ rather than a
separate form; a canonical form pins down the redundant operation slots.
Composing inside one index is strictly more expressive than composing
across two, which would need an intermediate prover word and a Zero
constraint to define it — sign-extension of a sub-word field, bit-field
extraction, and masking a byte off one end and back all become single
index entries.

The indicators compose because for each $(i, s)$ at most one input bit
$j$ has $\textsf{shift-ind}_\text{op}(i,j,s) = 1$. The composition
identity carries an index $k$ over the bits of the intermediate word,
which is never materialized — the reduction carries it as one more
sumcheck variable.

## Verifier

$Z_\text{cons}$ gains axes for the second slot. The claim is a sum over
$36 + \ell_\text{words}$ variables, still degree 2 in each, since every
variable occurs in exactly two of the five factors:

| variable | factors |
|---|---|
| $I$ | $\widetilde\delta_D$, outer indicator |
| $K$ | outer indicator, inner indicator |
| $J$ | inner indicator, $\widetilde w$ |
| $S_1$, $O_1$ | $\widetilde Z_\text{cons}$, inner indicator |
| $S_2$, $O_2$ | $\widetilde Z_\text{cons}$, outer indicator |
| $Y$ | $\widetilde Z_\text{cons}$, $\widetilde w$ |

Binding order is $O_2, S_2, O_1, S_1, J, K, I, Y$ — outer shift ahead of
inner. The verifier closes on four factors it evaluates itself, two of
them shift-indicator evaluations.

## Prover: six phases

The factored $h$ spans 24 variables, so its value table would hold
$2^{24}$ entries. The prover never forms it. Two successive $2^{15}$
tables stand in, both built by one operator:

$$T[\psi](J, S, O) := \sum_{k} \psi(k) \cdot
\widetilde{\textsf{shift-ind}}(k, J, S, O)$$

Every $(s,o)$ slice of $T[\psi]$ is a shift of $\psi$ (with a running
prefix sum for `sra`); the whole table costs $O(2^{15})$, a single slice
$O(2^6)$. Both contractions in $h$ are applications of it, since both
contract on the indicator's first index: $\eta := T[d]$ on the oblong
weights, and $h(J, s_2, o_2, s_1, o_1) = T[\eta(\cdot, s_2, o_2)](J,
s_1, o_1)$.

| phase | binds | cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $O_2$, $S_2$ (outer) | $2^{15}$ fixed + $O(2^6 \cdot
n_\text{shift})$ per round |
| 2 | $O_1$, $S_1$ (inner) | sparse–dense against $T[\psi]$ |
| 3 | $J$ | $O(2^6)$ |
| 4 | $K$ | $O(2^6)$ |
| 5 | $I$ | $O(2^6)$ |
| 6 | $Y$ | linear in the witness |

Phase 1 folds $\eta$ densely and derives each live active quadruple's
64-vector as one slice of $T$ applied to one stride of the folded
$\eta$. Phase 2 runs against $T[\psi]$, where $\psi$ is $\eta$'s
terminal fold.

### Why the outer shift binds first

Two independent reasons, both stated in the text:

- **Correctness.** $h = \delta^\top A_\text{outer} A_\text{inner}$,
whereas the nested-$T$ construction produces $\delta^\top A_\text{first}
A_\text{second}$. These agree only when the first-bound pair is the
outer one — the indicator matrices do not commute, `sra` being the
obstruction.
- **Cost.** The push-through is a shift only while the *other* pair is
still a cube index. Under the opposite order the outer indicator arrives
folded to a dense $2^6 \times 2^6$ matrix, costing a matrix–vector
product per active quadruple in place of a shift.

### No divisions

Every scalar the later phases need is a terminal fold: $G$ from $g$,
$\psi$ from $\eta$ (the terminal fold of $\eta$ *is* $\sum_i
d(i)\widetilde{\textsf{shift-ind}}(i, K, r_{s_2}, r_{o_2})$, the
multilinear extension commuting with the finite sum over $i$), and the
shift-indicator scalar from $\chi$. Only $\chi$ and $v$ are computed, at
$2^6$ succinct evaluations each.

$n_\text{shift}$ now counts active quadruples out of $2^{18}$, and the
sparse index is keyed by the quadruple.

the two pre-existing warnings (missing `csquotes`, no `\author`).

@@ -61,7 +61,7 @@ \subsection{Motivation}
 
 A \emph{succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge}, or SNARK, lets a verifier check the result of a computation far more cheaply than re-executing it, while remaining convinced---up to a negligible soundness error---that the prover holds a witness for which the computation was carried out correctly. SNARKs are the central primitive of \emph{verifiable computing}~\cite{Setty:2020aa}: a small, trusted device can audit the output of an untrusted, possibly faulty, and far more powerful one. When the argument additionally reveals nothing about the witness beyond the truth of the statement, it is \emph{zero-knowledge}, the property that underpins privacy-preserving applications such as verifiable credentials and confidential transactions.
 
-Many of the computations one most wants to prove---hash functions such as SHA-256, SHA-3, and Blake3, block ciphers, and the bit manipulation at the core of cryptographic primitives---are naturally expressed as operations on machine words: $64$-bit XOR, AND, shifts, rotations, and integer multiplication. General-purpose SNARKs built over large prime fields can prove such operations only after an expensive bit-by-bit decomposition, and even most binary-field systems pay a cost per individual bit. Binius64 instead takes the $64$-bit word as its unit of arithmetization. The constraint system (\S\ref{sec:constraint-system}) offers exactly four native constraint forms---\emph{Zero}, the vanishing of an XOR-accumulation of shifted words; \emph{BitAnd}, a bitwise AND between two such accumulations; \emph{IntMul}, an unsigned $64$-bit integer multiplication; and \emph{BinMul}, a multiplication in the GHASH field $\FF{2^{128}}$---and derives the remaining common operations (NOT, OR, integer addition and subtraction; \S\ref{sec:common-ops}) from them.
